etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 前(まえ) (mae, “front”), literally "honourable presence in front of me". Originally a polite pronoun applied to highly respected persons such as emperors or gods.
First attested in the early 900s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/omae/ → /omeː/
Corruption of お前(まえ) (omae). First attested in 1777.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ideku/ → /deku/ → /dekuru/ → /dekiru/
Originally appears in the Man'yōshū of 759 CE and other Old Japanese texts as 出(い)で来(く) (ideku), as a compound of 出(い)で (ide, “going out”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 出(い)づ (izu, ancient idu, ancient form of modern 出(で)る (deru, “to come out, to go out”))) + 来(く) (ku, “to come”, the ancient form of modern 来(く)る (kuru, “to come”)). The original meaning was “to come out”, extending in figurative contexts to a sense of “to appear, to become manifest”.
Phonologically, ideku shifted to deku by the mid-1400s in the Muromachi period, as the low-tone initial i dropped out, vaguely similar to the way that unstressed syllables in English may disappear. This deku then underwent a common shift in Muromachi Japanese to become dekuru, where all bigrade verbs and irregular verbs underwent a shift that included a -ru on the end of the plain form, in part through a fusion of the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) that has always ended in -ru for these verbs, and the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “terminal form”) that is used at the end of sentences.
As a later part of this same shift, the central vowel shifted from -u- to -i- to produce dekiru, as the main vowel -i- for the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) came to be used for all conjugated forms.
Over this same period, the meaning gradually shifted from “to come out” to include “to appear, to become manifest”, and from there “to come into existence anew”. This then extended further to “to occur, to happen; to be born; to be created, to be produced”, and thence “to come to fruition; to be completed, to be finished (with positive overtones)”. The underlying sense of latent existence gave rise to the meaning of “to be capable of making or producing something”, and then simply “to be able to do”.
In slang contexts in the early 1800s, dekiru came to mean “to have sex”, perhaps similar to the development of the English phrases “to do it, to get some, to get it on”.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: This etymology is hypothetical. Since that 無茶 (mucha) shifted to 滅茶 (mecha) by ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)), there may be an idea raised that a 滅茶 (mecha) ("ruined tea" or thus, "wrongly prepared tea") would be a 苦茶 (kucha) ("bitter tea"), which would also favor the sense of four-character idioms or 四字熟語 (yojijukugo).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Emphatic pronunciation of やはり (yahari); possibly an older form, see that entry for more.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English center, centre.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from French centi-, possibly via English centi-.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Clipping of センチメンタル (senchimentaru), in turn borrowed from English sentimental.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Internationalism; see English video.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 一(いち) (ichi, “one”) + 時(じ) (ji, “o'clock”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 一(いち) (ichi, “one”) + 時(じ) (ji, “time”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 一(いち) (ichi, “one”) + 時(とき) (toki, “time”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 一般 (ʔjit pan, “ordinary, common, general”, literally “one + sort”). Compare modern Mandarin reading yībān, Hakka yit-pân.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨yo₂⟩ → /yo/
From Old Japanese. The pronunciation is distinct from 夜 (/⁠yo₁⁠/, “night, nighttime”).
Change in meaning of 節 (yo), in the sense of the bamboos and reeds bulging at certain intervals.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 世 (MC syejH). The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Classical Japanese verb のす (nosu). Cognate with Japanese 載(の)せる (noseru).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Orthographic borrowing from Chinese 以上 (yǐshàng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Analyzed by references as either a compound of 再来 (sarai, “two next, the one after next”) + 週 (shū, “week”), or a compound of 再 (sa, “again, one more”) + 来週 (raishū, “next week”).
First attested in 1966.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 加 (“add, increase”) + 速度 (“speed, velocity”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 單位 (tan hwijᴴ).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ufasa/ → /uwasa/
First attested in works from the Muromachi period.
Considering that the meaning originally referred to private conversation about one's social superiors, possibly derived as a compound of 上 (ufa, “up, upward”, ancient reading of modern uwa, the combining form of modern ue; in reference to those of higher social standing) + さ (sa, “-ness”, suffix indicating state or degree).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Short form of the ateji spelling 土耳古(トルコ) (Toruko).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 土 (MC duX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compare with Okinawan 大家 (ufuyā).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 為合わす, 仕合わす (shiawasu, “to put together well; to work together well”, lower bigrade, with continuative form ending in -e), itself a compound of Old Japanese verbs 為 (su, “to do, to make something be a certain way”) + 合わす (awasu, “to join together, to fit together”).
Often spelled 幸せ with the final せ to indicate the reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 必 (hitsu, “necessary”) + 死 (shi, “death”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Appeared in the 1881 work 哲学字彙 (Tetsugaku Jii, “Dictionary of Philosophy”) by Inoue Tetsujirō as a translation of English abstract, as opposed to concrete.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: First attested in 1729.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 最 (sai-, “most”) + 近 (kin, “close”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Man'yōshū completed in 759.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 末 (MC mat).
First attested in Japanese in 1120.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Orthographic borrowing from Literary Chinese 熱帶／热带 (rèdài, literally “heat, high temperature + belt, zone, area”), which was coined by missionaries in China.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 物(もの) (mono-, “somehow; very”) + 凄(すご)い (sugoi, “terrible; amazing”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First attested in the late 11th century.
Sound shift from 盛(さか)り (sakari), the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 盛(さか)る (sakaru, “to be in prime condition”), itself sharing a root with 栄(さか)える (sakaeru, “to thrive, to boom”) and 咲(さ)く (saku, “to bloom”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 眺(なが)める (nagameru, “to gaze at”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
* /fafaki/ → /fawaki/ → /fauki/ → /fɔːki/ → /hoːki/
Alteration of hahaki. First cited to a text from 1496.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 羽 (ha, “feather; wing”) + 掃き (haki, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 掃(は)く (haku, “to sweep”).).
First cited to a text from 807.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Appears to be a shift from older shinbun reading, replacing the on'yomi of shin for 身 with the kun'yomi of mi. First attested in 1688.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowing from Middle Chinese 身分 (MC syin pjun|bjunH), modern Chinese spelling 身份 (shēnfèn). First attested in Japanese in 984. Superseded by the mibun reading starting from the late 1600s. The shinbun reading is included in a dictionary published in 1874, but it is not included in most modern references.
